drills.q: What two conditions must the fast/slow loop guard check, and why both?
drills.a: fast != null AND fast.next != null. Advancing fast requires computing fast.next.next, so both fast and fast.next must be non-null or the dereference crashes.

drills.q: After slow and fast meet inside a cycle, which pointer resets to head, and how fast does each pointer move afterward?
drills.a: Only ONE pointer resets to head (the other stays at the meeting point). After the reset, both pointers advance ONE step at a time -- not the original 2x speed.

drills.q: Prove that once both pointers are inside a cycle of length c, they must eventually meet.
drills.a: Each iteration, fast advances 2 nodes and slow advances 1, so the gap between them (measured going forward around the cycle) shrinks by exactly 1 node per iteration. Since the gap is initially at most c-1 and shrinks by 1 each step without ever jumping past 0 (it can't skip because it only decreases by 1), it must hit exactly 0 within at most c-1 further iterations -- i.e. they meet.

drills.q: Derive why resetting one pointer to head and advancing both by 1 step finds the cycle start. Use a = head-to-start distance, b = start-to-meeting distance, c = meeting-to-start distance (going forward around the cycle).
drills.a: At the meeting point, slow traveled a+b total steps, and fast traveled a+b+k(b+c) for some integer k>=1 (k full extra laps). Since fast always covers exactly 2x slow's distance: 2(a+b) = a+b+k(b+c), so a+b = k(b+c), giving a = k(b+c) - b = (k-1)(b+c) + c. This says a and c are congruent modulo the cycle length (b+c), so walking a steps from head lands on the same node as walking c steps from the meeting point -- exactly what advancing both pointers by 1 step simultaneously computes.

drills.q: A candidate solves Find the Duplicate Number using Floyd's algorithm but starts both slow and fast pointers at index nums[0] instead of index 0. Does this still work, and why or why not?
drills.a: It should start both at a fixed known entry point (conventionally index 0, treated as the 'head', not itself part of the value range needing dereference issues) and apply next(i) = nums[i]. Starting at nums[0] instead of 0 effectively skips the first hop of the implicit list; since the algorithm's correctness only depends on the sequence eventually entering the cycle (which it will regardless of a valid starting index within the array), starting at nums[0] still works as long as it's used consistently for both phases, but starting at index 0 is the standard, unambiguous choice and avoids off-by-one confusion in phase 2's head reset.

drills.q: Design a solution to Circular Array Loop (LC457) using fast/slow pointers, and explain what extra validation is needed beyond plain cycle detection.
drills.a: For each starting index i, define next(i) = (i + nums[i]) mod n, and run fast/slow to detect a meeting point. Beyond the meeting-point check, you must additionally validate: (1) the cycle length is greater than 1 (a self-loop where nums[i] mod n == 0 is explicitly disallowed), and (2) all steps along the cycle move in a consistent direction (all values in the cycle positive, or all negative) -- a direction change midway invalidates the loop per the problem's rules. Plain Floyd's detects a meeting point but doesn't validate either of these extra constraints.

drills.q: Explain the difference between the fast/slow (2x speed) pattern and the fixed-gap two-pointer pattern used in Remove Nth Node From End of List, and why conflating them fails.
drills.a: Fast/slow uses a speed DIFFERENTIAL (fast moves 2 steps per 1 slow step), useful for finding midpoints or cycles via relative closing rates. Remove Nth From End uses a fixed HEAD-START gap (lead pointer advances n steps first, then lead and trail advance together at the SAME speed), useful for finding a position a fixed distance from the end. Using a 2x speed ratio for the 'remove nth from end' problem doesn't produce a pointer at a fixed distance from the end -- it would land at a position determined by the list's total length divided by a ratio, not by the specific offset n the problem asks for.

drills.q: A candidate implements Palindrome Linked List by finding the middle, reversing the second half, comparing, and returning the boolean result -- without re-reversing the second half afterward. What's the correctness risk, and how would you detect it in code review?
drills.a: If any caller or subsequent test relies on the list being unmodified after the palindrome check (a common implicit expectation, and sometimes an explicit interview requirement), this silently corrupts the list's structure -- a real production bug pattern (a read-only-seeming operation mutating shared state). In code review, check whether the function's contract documents in-place mutation; if not, require restoring the original list (re-reverse the second half and re-attach) before returning, or operate on a scratch copy of the second half's values instead of physically reversing the node links.
